title: 2.7.2 Individual PA Part 2: In Your Own Words
description: Three short-answer questions. You explain the concepts in your own words. AI-graded.

aiGrader.rubricTitle: Chapter 2 Individual PA Part 2: In Your Own Words
aiGrader.prompt:
The student answers three short-answer questions in their own words. Grade each answer against its rubric. Be strict about correctness but generous with phrasing -- students are 14-year-olds explaining concepts in their own words. Do not deduct for minor grammar or spelling. Focus on whether the core idea is correct.

Question 1: Explain the difference between `for` and `while` loops. When would you choose one over the other?
Expected: `for` is for when you know how many iterations (or have a clear range with start, limit, step). `while` is for when you don't know the count in advance and loop until a condition changes. Key distinction: `for` packages the counter setup, condition, and step in the header; `while` only has the condition.

rubric.title: Explains when to use for vs while
rubric.description: Student identifies that `for` is for known iteration counts/ranges, `while` for unknown counts/condition-driven loops. Mentions that `for` packages init/condition/step in the header.

rubric.title: Explains why `===` is safer than `==`
rubric.description: Student explains that `===` compares both value AND type (strict equality), while `==` does type coercion which can cause surprising results (e.g., `0 == false` is true). Recommends `===` as the default.

rubric.title: Explains what `throw` does differently from logging an error
rubric.description: Student explains that `throw` stops the normal flow and jumps to the nearest `catch` (or crashes the program if uncaught), while `console.log` just prints and continues. `throw` is for signaling that something is wrong in a way the program can respond to; logging is just for humans to read.
